## The answer is already in the text {#text-targets .ss-slide .ss-construction}

<p class="ss-kicker">02 · TEXT SUPPLIES ITS OWN TARGETS</p>
<p class="ss-instruction">Choose a word to withhold. The source sentence stays unchanged.</p>
<div class="ss-source-label">SOURCE TEXT · visible to us when constructing the example</div>
<div id="ss-source-picker" class="ss-tokens ss-source-picker" role="group" aria-label="Choose the position to withhold"></div>

```{=html}
<svg class="ss-split" viewBox="0 0 1320 105" role="img" aria-label="Construct two separate objects from the source: the model input and a target kept for comparison."><defs><marker id="ss-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10" fill="none" stroke="#17364a" stroke-width="1.5"/></marker></defs><path d="M660 5V35H400V92M660 35H1120V92" fill="none" stroke="#17364a" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#ss-arrow)"/><path d="M400 70V92" stroke="#17364a" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#ss-arrow)"/></svg>
<div class="ss-constructed">
<div class="ss-input"><span class="ss-label">MODEL INPUT</span><div id="ss-model-input" class="ss-tokens" aria-live="polite"></div><p>The selected word is withheld here.</p></div>
<div class="ss-target"><span class="ss-label">TARGET · KEPT SEPARATELY</span><strong id="ss-target-word" aria-live="polite">?</strong><button id="ss-reveal-target" type="button" aria-pressed="false">Reveal target</button></div>
</div>
<p class="ss-principle">We construct the question.<br><strong>The observed text supplies the answer.</strong></p>
```

<p class="ss-source">Berkeley CS288, PDF pp. 4–5: turn unlabeled text into prediction examples. Adapted from our earlier corpus interaction; exact text manipulation, not model inference.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. Connect to the preceding question: where do targets come from?
The source is a six-word teaching sentence, using words rather than subword tokens.
Initially position 6, mat, is selected. Read the source, then the constructed
input. Ask for the target before pressing Reveal target. It is mat because that
is what the source contained, not because it is the only possible completion.

Click cat, then sat. Every change constructs a different input/target pair from
unchanged source text. The selected position, not just the word type, matters.
The target is hidden from the audience only as a teaching reveal; the training
procedure already has it. The model receives the input, while the loss function
also receives the retained target. The diagram separates these two routes.

This standalone control reuses the original corpus demonstration's withheld-word
and target-reveal mechanism without loading its unrelated model diagnostics.
It is not BERT's random sampling recipe and does not imply a 15% masking rate.
No model runs, and no optimization occurs on this slide. Transition: “With the
same source sentence, could we ask a different kind of prediction question?”
:::

## Keep the text. Change the question. {#two-prediction-questions .ss-slide .ss-recipes}

<p class="ss-source-sentence"><span>SAME SOURCE</span>The cat sat on the mat</p>

```{=html}
<div class="ss-recipe-row">
<div class="ss-recipe-heading"><b>01</b><h3>Recover a missing word</h3><p>Left and right context</p></div>
<div class="ss-recipe-example"><span class="ss-label">MODEL INPUT</span><div class="ss-tokens"><span>The</span><span class="ss-gap">____</span><span>sat</span><span>on</span><span>the</span><span>mat</span></div></div>
<div class="ss-recipe-answer"><span class="ss-label">TARGET</span><strong>cat</strong></div>
</div>
<div class="ss-recipe-row">
<div class="ss-recipe-heading"><b>02</b><h3>Predict the next word</h3><p>Preceding context only</p></div>
<div class="ss-recipe-example"><span class="ss-label">MODEL INPUT</span><div class="ss-tokens"><span>The</span><span>cat</span><span>sat</span><span>on</span></div><p>The following words are not supplied.</p></div>
<div class="ss-recipe-answer"><span class="ss-label">TARGET</span><strong>the</strong></div>
</div>
<p class="ss-principle">The source is the same.<br><strong>What the model can see is different.</strong></p>
```

<p class="ss-source">Adapted from Stanford CS224N, PDF pp. 12–18, and Berkeley CS288, pp. 36 and 58. Word-level teaching examples; detailed BERT and GPT recipes follow later.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. Ask students to read each input before its target. In row 1, the
model receives words on both sides of the missing cat. In row 2, the model
receives only The cat sat on. It must predict the observed next word, the, and
cannot read the later mat. The sentence on top is the experiment designer's
source, not an extra input to the predictor.

This adapts Berkeley's paired masked/causal diagrams while keeping our own fixed
six-word example. Architectures, causal masks, training parallelism, and original
BERT corruption percentages are deliberately deferred. The conceptual distinction
here is the available information. The fact that The occurs earlier does not
expose the specific next position: repeated word types are different events.
The missing-word example is an interior gap, unlike the initial last-word gap.

Ask: “Which question can use the words after the answer's position?” Then ask
whether either target needed a human sentiment annotation. Both targets are
observed tokens from the corpus. Transition: “Now construct the pair yourselves.”
:::

## One sentence. How many training examples? {#build-pair-pause .ss-slide .ss-count-pause}

<p class="ss-source-sentence"><span>OUR ENTIRE CORPUS</span>The cat sat on the mat</p>

```{=html}
<div class="ss-count-positions" aria-label="Six word positions"><span><b>1</b>The</span><span><b>2</b>cat</span><span><b>3</b>sat</span><span><b>4</b>on</span><span><b>5</b>the</span><span><b>6</b>mat</span></div>
<div class="ss-pause-panel"><span class="ss-pause-badge">PAUSE · 45 SECONDS</span><h3>How many different input–target pairs can we extract?</h3><p><strong>The rule:</strong> withhold exactly one word position per example.<br>Keep every other word visible. Predict the original word.</p></div>
<div class="ss-count-task"><strong>Write two of your examples.</strong><p>Count positions—even when the same word appears more than once.</p></div>
```

<p class="ss-source">Reuses the counting activity from the preserved first draft, narrowed to one sentence. Word positions only; no punctuation, padding, or special tokens.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 2 minutes including a 45-second pause. Keep the same six-word sentence from
slides 10–11. We now fix the missing-word construction: withhold exactly one
position and keep all other words. We are not counting subsets of masked words,
next-token examples, or unique word types. Do not reveal the computed count here.

Ask students to write two explicit input/target pairs. The numbered positions
make the task inspectable. The repeated the belongs to different positions; we
count examples, not dictionary entries. The solution and simulation follow on
the next slide. This is the earlier draft's enumeration exercise, using a single
sentence rather than the three-sentence corpus.
:::

## Six positions, six training examples {#build-pair-solution .ss-slide .ss-enumeration}

<p class="ss-enumeration-lead">The cat sat on the mat <span>→ withhold one position at a time</span></p>

```{=html}
<div class="ss-enumeration-toolbar"><strong>1 sentence × 6 positions = 6 pairs</strong><button type="button" id="ss-next-example">Next example →</button></div>
<div class="ss-example-list" id="ss-example-list" role="group" aria-label="Inspect each of the six extracted training examples"></div>
<div class="ss-example-inspector" aria-live="polite"><div><span class="ss-label">SELECTED MODEL INPUT</span><p id="ss-enumerated-input">____ cat sat on the mat</p></div><div><span class="ss-label">TARGET TO PREDICT</span><strong id="ss-enumerated-target">The</strong></div></div>
<p class="ss-enumeration-takeaway">No new annotation. Each target was already in the sentence.</p>
```

<p class="ss-source">Interactive enumeration adapted from the first draft's pair-matrix simulation. Exact constructed examples, not model predictions or a training run; overlapping examples are not independent observations.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 4 minutes. Reveal the six generated pairs together. This restores the
original draft's clickable enumeration and input/target inspector for one sentence.
Click a row or use Next example to move the gap through every word position.
The source remains fixed, the input loses one word, and that original word becomes
the target. These are desired predictions, not outputs from an actual model.

Start at position 1 and advance through all six. Pause on positions 1 and 5:
The/the refer to distinct occurrences, so both yield a training example. The
capitalization here comes directly from the displayed sentence. Ask students to
compare their written pairs with the generated rows. No probability recap is
needed; students already know that a model produces an output distribution.

Six is a consequence of the stated one-hidden-position rule, not a universal
count for every self-supervised recipe. A different construction gives different
examples. BERT's actual sampling policy comes later. The six overlapping pairs
reuse one observed sentence, so do not call them six independent observations.
Transition: “Apply this construction to a corpus, and the text supplies targets
for a whole training loop.”
:::

## Text → examples → a learning signal {#self-supervision-bridge .ss-slide .ss-training-loop}

```{=html}
<svg class="ss-loop-diagram" viewBox="0 0 1320 440" role="img" aria-label="Source text supplies an input and a separate target. The input passes through the model to a prediction. The loss compares prediction and target, then gradients update model parameters.">
<defs><marker id="ss-loop-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10" fill="none" stroke="#17364a" stroke-width="1.5"/></marker></defs>
<g font-family="sans-serif" fill="#17364a"><rect x="15" y="115" width="250" height="165" rx="12" fill="#e5e2d9"/><text x="40" y="160" font-size="27" font-weight="bold">SOURCE TEXT</text><text x="40" y="205" font-size="27">…on the shelf</text><text x="40" y="238" font-size="22">many observed</text><text x="40" y="266" font-size="22">sentences</text>
<path d="M265 155H340V95H435M340 155V325H1000V260" fill="none" stroke="#17364a" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#ss-loop-arrow)"/><path d="M400 95H435" stroke="#17364a" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#ss-loop-arrow)"/>
<text x="355" y="55" font-size="24">input: …on the ____</text><text x="365" y="360" font-size="27">target: shelf</text>
<rect x="460" y="65" width="225" height="125" rx="12" fill="#d6e8e6"/><text x="572" y="116" font-size="30" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">MODEL θ</text><text x="572" y="155" font-size="23" text-anchor="middle">predict</text>
<path d="M690 125H820" stroke="#17364a" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#ss-loop-arrow)"/><text x="715" y="90" font-size="23">probabilities</text>
<rect x="845" y="65" width="380" height="195" rx="12" fill="#f1dfc2"/><text x="1035" y="115" font-size="31" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">LOSS</text><text x="1035" y="162" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle">compare prediction</text><text x="1035" y="202" font-size="26" text-anchor="middle">with the retained target</text>
<path d="M1150 265V410H570V200" fill="none" stroke="#0f7881" stroke-width="4" stroke-dasharray="10 7" marker-end="url(#ss-loop-arrow)"/><text x="790" y="399" font-size="24" fill="#0f7881">gradients update θ</text></g></svg>
<p class="ss-summary">Self-supervised learning <strong>still has targets</strong>.<br>We obtain them from the text instead of annotating each example.</p>
<div class="ss-next"><span>NEXT · BERT</span><p>How can a model read <strong>both sides</strong> of a word<br>without seeing the answer it must predict?</p></div>
```

<p class="ss-source">Original training-flow diagram. Based on Stanford CS224N, PDF pp. 11, 18–19, and Berkeley CS288, pp. 35–36. The target enters the loss, not the predictor.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. Trace the two routes from source text. One becomes the model
input. The other retains shelf for the loss. Prediction probabilities and the
observed target meet at the loss. Gradients then update the permitted model
parameters. The dashed return route expresses a dependency; it is not a measured
training trajectory. No inference, optimization, or timer runs in this diagram.

Scale the picture conceptually: repeat this construction across many sentences,
form batches, and repeat forward/loss/backward/update steps. The corpus supplies
observations without a person writing a separate task label for each prediction.
This does not remove decisions about corpus selection, preprocessing, or quality.
We have not manufactured new independent information by extracting overlapping
examples from the same sentence.

Synthesize the section: source, input, target; control access; compare prediction
with the retained target. The model can see a target through the loss during
learning without receiving it as input for that prediction. At ordinary inference,
there is no such target/loss/update loop unless we explicitly run training.

End with the question about using both sides without exposing the answer. The
next section formalizes the BERT task and its corruption choices. Stop here for
instructor review; no BERT content is newly authored in this increment.
:::
